answer.worked:

children.prompt: Find when the fund first exceeds $\$500\,000$.

answer.short: At the end of the 23rd year.
answer.worked:
After $n$ annual contributions:
$$\begin{aligned}FV_n&=10\,000(1.07)^{n-1}+10\,000(1.07)^{n-2}+\cdots+10\,000\\FV_n&=10\,000\left[\frac{1.07^n-1}{0.07}\right]\end{aligned}$$
For the fund to exceed $\$500\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned}10\,000\left[\frac{1.07^n-1}{0.07}\right]&>500\,000\\1.07^n&>4.5\\n&>\frac{\log(4.5)}{\log(1.07)}\\n&>22.230378\ldots\end{aligned}$$
The first whole number of contributions is 23. Checking the neighbouring years:
$$\begin{aligned}FV_{22}&\approx\$490\,057.39\\FV_{23}&\approx\$534\,361.41\end{aligned}$$
The fund first exceeds $\$500\,000$ at the end of the 23rd year.

children.prompt: What annual instalment would produce $\$1\,000\,000$ after 30 years?

answer.worked:
Let the end-of-year contribution be $a$. At 7% p.a., the 30 contributions form the series

entries.description: Types of Annuity Problems

Ordinary annuity
End-of-period contributions with end-of-period compounding.
\(FV=a\left[\frac{(1+r)^n-1}{(1+r)-1}\right]\)

Annuity due
Start-of-period contributions with end-of-period compounding.
Set up geometric series and multiply by one more of \((1+r)\):
\(FV=a\left[\frac{(1+r)^n-1}{(1+r)-1}\right](1+r)\)

Annuity with starting lump sum
Split account into two parts, the original lump sum, \(PV\), which earns compound interest separately, and the ordinary annuity of the regular contributions.
\(FV=PV(1+r)^n+a\left[\frac{(1+r)^n-1}{(1+r)-1}\right]\)

Annuity withdrawal problem:
Treat your starting amount as if you never touch it and continue to compound.
Treat your withdrawals as a parallel timeline and subtract: every time you take money out, you lose out on the future interest that specific cash would have earned.
\(FV=PV(1+r)^n-a\left[\frac{(1+r)^n-1}{(1+r)-1}\right]\)
